source_text:
Στίχ. με΄. Καὶ ὁ λεπρὸς, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀφὴ, τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ ἔσται παραλελυμένα, καὶ ἡ κεφαλὴ αὐτοῦ ἀκάλυπτος.
Διατί τοῦ λεπροῦ ἀκάλυπτον εἶναι κελεύει τὴν κεφαλὴν, καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια παραλελυμένα; Ἵνα γνωριστὸς ᾗ καὶ μὴ μετσλαγχάνωσι τῆς ἀκαθαρσίας οἱ προσπελάζοντες. Οὕτως ὁ Ἀπόστολος περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων ἔφη· Στέλλεσθε ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀδελφοῦ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντος, καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν, ἣν παρελάβετε παῤ ἡμῶν· καὶ, Ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος, ἢ πόρνος, ἢ πλεονέκτης, ἢ εἰδωλολάτρης, ἢ μέθυσος, ἢ λοίδορος, ἢ ἅρπαξ· τῷ τοιούτῳ μὴ συνεσθίειν (18).
thought_title: The leper's public marking as a model for separating from sinners
orientation: Origen is commenting on Leviticus 13:45, where the law prescribes how a leper must appear in public, and he connects this to the Apostle's command to avoid sinful brothers.
pass_a_gloss: Verse 45. And the leper in whom is the touch, his garments shall be loosened, and his head uncovered. Why does he command the head of the leper to be uncovered, and the garments loosened? So that he may be recognizable and those approaching may not share in the uncleanness. Thus the Apostle said about those who sin: Keep yourselves away from every brother walking disorderly, and not according to the tradition which you received from us; and, If any brother is named, either a fornicator, or a greedy person, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or a reviler, or a robber; with such a one do not eat.

choices.why: The verb παραλύω means to loosen or let down; the garments hang loose rather than being torn or rent, matching the public dishevelment of the leper.
ἀφή is the noun for touch or contact, here the mark or spot of the disease on the skin; rendering it as 'the touch' preserves the literal sense of the source.
The middle imperative of στέλλω with ἀπό means to withdraw or keep oneself away from; this preserves the command's force.
The verb μεταλαγχάνω means to obtain a share of or partake in; the subjunctive with ἵνα expresses purpose.
ἀτάκτως is the adverb 'disorderly' modifying περιπατοῦντος 'walking'; this keeps the adverbial force rather than turning it into an adjective.

pass_b_english: Verse 45: “And the leper in whom is the plague of leprosy—his garments shall be loosened, and his head uncovered” (Leviticus 13:45). Why does it command that the leper’s head be uncovered and his garments loosened? So that he may be recognizable, and those who approach may not share in his uncleanness. Thus the Apostle said about sinners: “Keep yourselves away from every brother walking disorderly and not according to the tradition which you received from us” (2 Thessalonians 3:6), and, “If anyone named a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or a reviler, or a robber—do not eat with such a person” (1 Corinthians 5:11).
notes: The form μετσλαγχάνωσι appears to be a scribal error or variant for μεταλαγχάνωσι (from μεταλαγχάνω); the gloss assumes the intended verb is μεταλαγχάνω.

problems.ruling: ἀφὴ in Lev 13:45 means plague/affliction, not 'touch'; 'in whom is the touch' misleads readers

edits.new: in whom there is a blemish

fixed: Changed 'in whom is the touch' to 'in whom there is a blemish': Greek ἀφὴ here means 'blemish/defect', not 'touch'.

problems.quote: the one who became a Jew in order to gain Jews, and circumcised Timothy
problems.why: Reader may not connect 'the one who became a Jew' with Paul 'the Apostle'.
problems.fix: Identify both as Paul up front.

problems.quote: Verse 45: “And the leper in whom there is a blemish—his garments shall be loosened, and his head uncovered” (Leviticus 13:45)
problems.why: Lev 13:45 LXX says 'the plague of leprosy,' not 'a blemish'; 'blemish' is a different Hebrew term.
problems.fix: Render as 'in whom is the plague of leprosy.'

fixed: The English 'in whom there is a blemish' misstates the source ἀφή, which in Lev 13:45 LXX refers to the plague of leprosy, not a blemish; changed to 'in whom is the plague of leprosy'.
